mil6.2.8:0.4: 8. The Method of Promulgating the Rules
mil6.2.8:1.1: “Sir Nagasena, those who in former times were the teachers of the physicians were like this—
mil6.2.8:1.2: Narada, Dhammantari, Angiraso, Kapilo, Kandaraggi, Samo, Atulo, Pubbakaccayano. All those teachers, knowing that alone entirely, without remainder, the arising of illness, its cause, its nature, its onset, its treatment, its procedure, and its success and failure: ‘such and such illnesses will arise in this body’—with a single stroke they marked off a span and bound it into a Sutta. All of them lacked omniscience. So why, when the Tathagata, the all-knowing, had known through his knowledge as a Buddha what act was to come, and had determined ‘in this situation such and such a training rule is to be prescribed’—why did he not prescribe a training rule without remainder, and only when the situation had arisen, among human beings fallen into distress, into matured distress, into severe distress, into helpless condition, prescribe a training rule for his disciples at that very time”?
mil6.2.8:2.1: “That, Great King, was known to the Tathagata: ‘at that time, among these people, more than a hundred and fifty training rules are to be prescribed’. And the Tathagata thought: ‘if I prescribe more than a hundred and fifty training rules in a single stroke, the great mass of people will be overcome by fatigue: “there is so much here to be kept, it is hard indeed for a person to go forth in the ascetic Gotama’s teaching”. Those who want to go forth will not go forth, they will not have faith in my words, and those people who have no faith in them will be led to ruin. So I shall wait until the situation has arisen, and then, having explained the teaching and prescribed a training rule for those fallen into matured distress, I shall prescribe it””.
mil6.2.8:3.1: “Amazing, sir Nagasena, of the Buddhas! Astonishing, sir Nagasena, of the Buddhas! So great is the Tathagata’s knowledge of omniscience. This, sir Nagasena, was well considered by the Tathagata: hearing ‘there is so much here to be learned’, the seven would be overcome by fatigue, and not even one would go forth in the teaching of the Jinas. I accept this exactly as it is”.
mil6.2.8:4.1: The Method of Promulgating the Rules, eighth.
